entries.b9b038f1a046ee753215e6d392579ce7f1c4ac67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6868"/><div sID="gen10535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6868"/><hi type="bold">25. Save now--</hi>Hebrew, "Hosanna" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">Psa 115:2</reference>, &c., as to now) a form of prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">Psa 20:9</reference>), since, in our use, of praise. <div eID="gen10535" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6e157c87df022409f88b9d0e5d4693c533b6c3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6869"/><div sID="gen10536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6869"/><hi type="bold">26. he that cometh ... Lord--</hi>As above intimated, this may be applied to the visible head of the Jewish Church entering the sanctuary, as leading the procession; typically it belongs to Him of whom the phrase became an epithet (Mal 3:1; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mt 21:9</reference>). <div eID="gen10536" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f2a083bcd0118bf5566ec9a0a463be7e5e4a3b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6870"/><div sID="gen10537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6870"/><hi type="bold">27-29. showed us light--</hi>or favor (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">97:11</reference>). With the sacrificial victim brought bound to the altar is united the more spiritual offering of praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">23</reference>), expressed in the terms with which the Psalm opened. <chapter eID="Ps.118"/>

entries.b168d49c2fa84e1f5e23dc09d248c02e0df0f011: <div eID="gen22657" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22658" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22659" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22659" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22658" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22660" type="x-p"/> A general exhortation to praise God for his mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.1-Psa.118.4">Psa 118:1-4</reference>. The psalmist, by his own experience, encourages the people to trust in God, and shows them the advantage of it, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.5-Psa.118.9">Psa 118:5-9</reference>; then describes his enemies, and shows how God enabled him to destroy them, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.10-Psa.118.13">Psa 118:10-13</reference>. The people rejoice on the account, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.15">Psa 118:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.16">Psa 118:16</reference>. He speaks again of the help he received from the Lord; and desires admission into the temple, that he may enter and praise the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.17-Psa.118.19">Psa 118:17-19</reference>. The gate is opened, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.20">Psa 118:20</reference>. He offers praise, 21. The priests, etc., acknowledge the hand of the Lord in the deliverance wrought, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.22-Psa.118.24">Psa 118:22-24</reference>. The psalmist prays for prosperity, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.25">Psa 118:25</reference>. The priest performs his office, blesses the people, and all join in praise, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.26">Psa 118:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.27">Psa 118:27</reference>. The psalmist expresses his confidence, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.28">Psa 118:28</reference>. The general doxology, or chorus, <reference osisRef="Psa.118.29">Psa 118:29</reference>. <div eID="gen22660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22661" type="x-p"/> Most probably David was the author of this Psalm, though many think it was written after the captivity. It partakes of David's spirit, and every where shows the hand of a master. The style is grand and noble; the subject, majestic. <div eID="gen22661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22662" type="x-p"/> Dr. Kennicott, who joins this and the hundred and seventeenth Psalm together, considers the whole as a dialogue, and divides it accordingly. The whole of the hundred and seventeenth he gives to the psalmist as part the first, with the first four verses of the hundred and eighteenth. The second part, which is from the fifth verse to the twenty-first inclusive, he gives to the Messiah. The third part, from the twenty-second verse to the twenty-seventh, he gives to the chorus. And the fourth part, the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth verses, he gives to the psalmist. Of the whole he has given an improved version. <div eID="gen22662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22663" type="x-p"/> Bishop Horsley is still different. He considers the hundred and seventeenth Psalm as only the exordium of this. The whole poem, he states, is a triumphant processional song. The scene passes at the front gate of the temple. A conqueror with his train appears before it; he demands admittance to return thanks for his deliverance and final success, in an expedition of great difficulty and danger. The conqueror and his train sing the hundred and seventeenth Psalm, and the first four verses of the hundred and eighteenth, as they advance to the gate of the temple, in this manner - The hundred and seventeenth Psalm, Chorus of the whole procession. The first verse of the hundred and eighteenth Psalm, A single voice. The second, Another single voice. The third, A third single voice. The fourth, Chorus of the whole procession. Arrived at the temple gate, the conqueror alone sings the fifth, sixth, and seventh verses. The eighth and ninth are sung by his train in chorus. The conqueror, again alone, sings the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth verses. His train, in chorus, sing the fifteenth and sixteenth. The conqueror alone sings the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth verses. The twentieth is sung by the priests and Levites within, in chorus. The twenty-fifth by the conqueror alone within the gates. The twenty-sixth, by the priests and Levites in chorus. The twenty-seventh, by the conqueror's train in chorus. The twenty-eighth, by the conqueror alone. The twenty-ninth, by the united chorus of priests and Levites, and the conqueror's train, all within the gates. "Now," the learned bishop adds, "the Jewish temple was a type of heaven; the priests within represent the angelic host attending round the throne of God in heaven; the Conqueror is Messiah; and his train, the redeemed." On this distribution the bishop has given a new version. The simple distribution into parts, which I have given in the contents, is, in my opinion, the best. Ingenious as Dr. Kennicott and Bishop Horsley are, they seem to me too mechanical. This is the last of those Psalms which form the great hallel, which the Jews sung at the end of the passover.
entries.b01f4b8f1f84212fc02d5436bc9df890aa95b511: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22664" type="x-p"/> Let Israel now say - Seeing the hand of the Lord so visibly, and the deliverance gained, that God's mercy endureth for ever.
entries.79409657afb64ce5e8f016e3c057b15a4ae19f93: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22665" type="x-p"/> The house of Aaron - The priesthood is still preserved, and the temple worship restored.
entries.e7754c0ae66dd7b3ffd37e22e4c34c3024815ff8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22666" type="x-p"/> That fear the Lord - All sincere penitents and genuine believers. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.115.9-Psa.115.11">Psa 115:9-11</reference> (note).
entries.c28754c3a532dca735f8e8aaa36569d60e45fa11: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22667" type="x-p"/> I called upon the Lord - I am a standing proof and living witness of God's mercy. Take encouragement from me.
entries.153de52bf82dba7205f836c54a9f2e2cb389db04: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22668" type="x-p"/> The Lord taketh my part with them that help me - Literally, The Lord is to me among my helpers. Therefore shall I see my desire upon them that hate me. Literally, And I shall look among them that hate me. As God is on my side, I fear not to look the whole of them in the face. I shall see them defeated.
entries.56bf76a84d7d61192a44f094cb38b065cfc66a13: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22669" type="x-p"/> Better to trust in the Lord - Man is feeble, ignorant, fickle, and capricious; it is better to trust in Jehovah than in such.
entries.fa135d4782e35a57ccbf1ac69dc1f14fcbd1c79b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22670" type="x-p"/> In princes - Men of high estate are generally proud, vainglorious, self-confident, and rash: it is better to trust in God than in them. Often they cannot deliver, and often they will not when they can. However, in the concerns of our salvation, and in matters which belong to Providence, they can do nothing.
entries.4b19948f06b47f28bb1dd34f782cbde880499e3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22671" type="x-p"/> All nations compassed me about - This is by some supposed to relate to David, at the commencement of his reign, when all the neighboring Philistine nations endeavored to prevent him from establishing himself in the kingdom. Others suppose it may refer to the Samaritans, Idumeans, Ammonites, and others, who endeavored to prevent the Jews from rebuilding their city and their temple after their return from captivity in Babylon. <div eID="gen22671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22672" type="x-p"/> But in the name of the Lord will I destroy them - Dr. Kennicott renders אמילם amilam, "I shall disappoint them;" Bishop Horsley, "I cut them to pieces;" Mr. N. Berlin, repuli eas, "I have repelled them." "I will cut them off;" Chaldee. Ultus sum in eos, "I am avenged on them;" Vulgate. So the Septuagint.
entries.845766d56ef4524e22ebd082d30521455515b7b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22673" type="x-p"/> They compassed me about like bees; they are quenched as the fire of thorns - I shall refer to Dr. Delaney's note on this passage. The reader has here in miniature two of the finest images in Homer; which, if his curiosity demands to be gratified, he will find illustrated and enlarged, Iliad ii., ver. 86. - Επεσσευοντο δε λαοι. Ηΰτε εθνεα εισι μελισσαων αδιναων, Πετρης εκ γλαφυρης αιει νεον ερχομεναων, Βοτρυδον δε πετονται επ' ανθεσιν ειαρινοισιν, Αἱ μεν τ' ενθα ἁλις πεποτηαται, αἱ δε τε ανθα Ὡς των εθνεα πολλα νεων απο και κλισιαων Ηΐονος προπαροιθε βαθειης εστιχοωντο Ιλαδον εις αγορην. - The following host, <div eID="gen22673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22674" type="x-p"/> Poured forth by thousands, darkens all the coast. <div eID="gen22674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22675" type="x-p"/> As from some rocky cleft the shepherd sees, <div eID="gen22675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22676" type="x-p"/> Clustering in heaps on heaps, the driving bees, <div eID="gen22676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22677" type="x-p"/> Rolling and blackening, swarms succeeding swarms, <div eID="gen22677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22678" type="x-p"/> With deeper murmurs and more hoarse alarms: <div eID="gen22678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22679" type="x-p"/> Dusky they spread a close embodied crowd, <div eID="gen22679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22680" type="x-p"/> And o'er the vale descends the living cloud; <div eID="gen22680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22681" type="x-p"/> So from the tents and ships a lengthening train <div eID="gen22681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22682" type="x-p"/> Spreads all the beach, and wide o'ershades the plain; <div eID="gen22682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22683" type="x-p"/> Along the region runs a deafening sound; <div eID="gen22683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22684" type="x-p"/> Beneath their footsteps groans the trembling ground. <div eID="gen22684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22685" type="x-p"/> Pope <div eID="gen22685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22686" type="x-p"/> The other image, the fire consuming the thorns, we find in the same book, ver. 455: - Ηΰτε πυρ αΐδηλον επιφλεγει ασπετον ὑλην, Ουρεος εν κορυφης· ἑκαθεν δε τε φαινεται αυγη· Ὡς των ερχομενων, απο χαλκου θεσπεσιοιο Αιγλη παμφανοωσα δι' αιθερος ουρανον ἱκεν. <div eID="gen22686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22687" type="x-p"/> As on some mountain, through the lofty grove, <div eID="gen22687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22688" type="x-p"/> The crackling flames ascend and blaze above; <div eID="gen22688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22689" type="x-p"/> The fires expanding, as the winds arise, <div eID="gen22689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22690" type="x-p"/> Shoot their long beams, and kindle half the skies; <div eID="gen22690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22691" type="x-p"/> So, from the polished arms, and brazen shields, <div eID="gen22691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22692" type="x-p"/> A gleamy splendor flashed along the fields. <div eID="gen22692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22693" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen22693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22694" type="x-p"/> The arms resembling a gleaming fire is common both to the psalmist and Homer; but the idea of that fire being quenched when the army was conquered, is peculiar to the psalmist.
entries.a50bf616216142a68ded3c8583189e53121c00f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22695" type="x-p"/> Thou hast thrust sore at me - In pushing thou hast pushed me that I might fall. <div eID="gen22695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22696" type="x-p"/> But the Lord helped me - Though he possessed skill, courage, and strength, yet these could not have prevailed had not God been his helper; and to him he gives the glory of the victory.
entries.a9e5387f39bd372616c48a48813388132564fee8: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22697" type="x-p"/> The voice of rejoicing - Formerly there was nothing but wailings; but now there is universal joy because of the salvation - the deliverance, which God has wrought for us.
entries.a6c4d4ea089047b6141968f55631635f41549bfc: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22698" type="x-p"/> The right hand of the Lord is exalted - Jehovah lifted up his right hand, and with it performed prodigies of power.
entries.6dea359810db77096c556c3fb4da080144b825af: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22699" type="x-p"/> I shall not die - I was nigh unto death; but I am preserved, - preserved to publish the wondrous works of the Lord.
entries.4ef2a1b0da5531d0765d56f5f53c4c5dc08671a1: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22700" type="x-p"/> Open to me the gates - Throw open the doors of the temple, that I may enter and perform my vows unto the Lord.
entries.db3ae2d0733d2fa8c402daee3b5a3ce227ca727e: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen22700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22701" type="x-p"/> This gate of the Lord - Supposed to be the answer of the Levites to the request of the king.
entries.70b30653daf51ea96f766977011dda27ae6c6e0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen22701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22702" type="x-p"/> I will praise thee - He is now got within the gates, and breaks out into thanksgivings for the mercies he had received. He is become my salvation - he himself hath saved me from all mine enemies.
entries.c33f70f4c7e1f541cbdb92079c64fa8bfe7ff30f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> , <reference osisRef="Psa.118.23">Psa 118:23</reference> <div eID="gen22702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22703" type="x-p"/> The stone which the builders refused - See a full elucidation of these two verses in the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.21.42">Mat 21:42</reference> (note).
entries.ebda664fd81306b9a0ad9179acd9fc9411acfacf: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen22703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22704" type="x-p"/> This is the day which the Lord hath made - As the Lord hath called me to triumph, this is the day which he hath appointed for that purpose. This is a gracious opportunity; I will improve it to his glory.
entries.d56c8c3cf7f9da50e51cd8aaaf8ce29b1f2b1574: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen22704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22705" type="x-p"/> Save now, I beseech thee - These words were sung by the Jews on the feast of tabernacles, when carrying green branches in their hands; and from the הושיעה נא hoshiah nna, we have the word hosanna. This was sung by the Jewish children when Christ made his public entry into Jerusalem. See <reference osisRef="Mat.21.9">Mat 21:9</reference> (note), and see the note there, in which the word and the circumstance are both explained.
entries.627348a020d38c6f536a420aaf68e3011b413b75: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen22705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22706" type="x-p"/> We have blessed you - The answer of the Levities to the king.
entries.070c09836c3dacae5e6d84804e3c02af5965c967: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen22706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22707" type="x-p"/> God is the Lord - Rather אל יהוה El Yehovah, the strong God Jehovah. <div eID="gen22707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22708" type="x-p"/> Which hath showed us light - ויאר לנו vaiyaer lanu, "And he will illuminate us." Perhaps at this time a Divine splendor shone upon the whole procession; a proof of God's approbation. <div eID="gen22708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22709" type="x-p"/> Bind the sacrifice with cords - The Chaldee paraphrases this verse thus: "Samuel the prophet said, Bind the little one with chains for a solemn sacrifice, until ye have sacrificed him and sprinkled his blood on the horns of the altar." It is supposed that the words refer to the feast of tabernacles, and חג chag here means the festival victim. Several translate the original "keep the festival with thick boughs of the horns of the altar." In this sense the Vulgate and Septuagint understood the passage. David in this entry into the temple was a type of our blessed Lord, who made a similar entry, as related <reference osisRef="Mat.21.8-Mat.21.10">Mat 21:8-10</reference>.
entries.fcaea8400ab18ac192d7d0aa700539766da28d3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen22709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22710" type="x-p"/> O give thanks unto the Lord - This is the general doxology or chorus. All join in thanksgiving, and they end as they began: "His mercy endureth for ever." It began at the creation of man; it will continue till the earth is burnt up.  <chapter eID="Ps.118"/> <div eID="gen22710" type="x-p"/>

entries.ea6e4ad4f1c63a69aa40cf12bda01d22ff4fe7dd: <div eID="gen10112" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Festival Psalm at the Dedication of the New Temple</title> <div sID="gen10113" type="x-p"/> What the close of <reference osisRef="Ps.117.1-Ps.117.2">Psa 117:1-2</reference> says of God’s truth, viz., that it endureth for ever, the beginning of Ps 118 says of its sister, His mercy or loving-kindness. It is the closing Psalm of the <hi type="italic">Hallel</hi>, which begins with <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>, and the third <hi type="italic">Hodu</hi> (vid., on Ps 105). It was Luther’s favourite Psalm: his beauteous <hi type="italic">Confitemini</hi>, which “had helped him out of troubles out of which neither emperor nor king, nor any other man on earth, could have helped him.” With the exposition of this his noblest jewel, his defence and his treasure, he occupied himself in the solitude of his Patmos. <div eID="gen10113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10114" type="x-p"/> It is without any doubt a post-exilic song. Here too Hupfeld sweeps away everything into vague generality; but the history of the period after the Exile, without any necessity for our coming down to the Maccabean period, as do De Wette and Hitzig, presents three occasions which might have given birth to it; viz., (1) The first celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles in the seventh month of the first year of the Return, when there was only a plain altar as yet erected on the holy place, Ezr 3:1-4 (to be distinguished from a later celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles on a large scale and in exact accordance with the directions of the Law, Neh. 8). So Ewald. (2) The laying of the foundation-stone of the Temple in the second month of the second year, Ezr 3:8. So Hengstenberg. (3) The dedication of the completed temple in the twelfth month of the sixth year of Darius, Ezr 6:15. So Stier. These references to contemporary history have all three more or less in their favour. The first if favoured more especially by the fact, that at the time of the second Temple <reference osisRef="Ps.118.25">Psa 118:25</reference> was the festal cry amidst which the altar of burnt-offering was solemnly compassed on the first six days of the Feast of Tabernacles once, and on the seventh day seven times. This seventh day was called the great Hosanna (<hi type="italic">Hosanna rabba</hi>), and not only the prayers for the Feast of Tabernacles, but even the branches of willow trees (including the myrtles) which are bound to the palm-branch (<hi type="italic">lulab</hi>), were called <hi type="italic">Hosannas</hi> (הושׁענות, Aramaic הושׁעני).<note placement="foot">Vid., my Talmudic Studies, vi. (<hi type="italic">Der Hosianna-Ruf</hi>), in the <hi type="italic">Lutherische Zeischrift</hi>, 1855, S. 653-656.</note> <div eID="gen10114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10115" type="x-p"/> The second historical reference is favoured by the fact, that the narrative appears to point directly to our Psalm when it says: <hi type="italic">And the builders laid the foundation of the Temple of Jahve, and the priests were drawn up there in official robes with trumpets, and the Levites the descendants of Asaph with cymbals, to praise Jahve after the direction of David king of Israel, and they sang</hi> על־ישׂראל בּהלּל וּבהודת ליהוה כּי טוב כּי־לעולם חסדּו; <hi type="italic">and all the people raised a great shout</hi> בּהלּל ליהוה, <hi type="italic">because the house of Jahve was founded</hi>. But both of these derivations of the Psalm are opposed by the fact that <reference osisRef="Ps.116.19">Psa 116:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.118.20">Psa 118:20</reference> assume that the Temple-building is already finished; whereas the unmistakeable allusions to the events that transpired during the building of the Temple, viz., the intrigues of the Samaritans, the hostility of the neighbouring peoples, and the capriciousness of the Persian kings, favour the third. In connection with this reference of the Psalm to the post-exilic dedication of the Temple, <reference osisRef="Ps.118.19-Ps.118.20">Psa 118:19-20</reference>, too, now present no difficulty. <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference> is better understood as spoken in the presence of the now upreared Temple-building, than as spoken in the presence of the foundation-stone; and the words “unto the horns of the altar” in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.27">Psa 118:27</reference>, interpreted in many different ways, come into the light of Ezr 6:17. <div eID="gen10115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10116" type="x-p"/> The Psalm falls into two divisions. The first division (vv. 1-19) is sung by the festive procession brought up by the priests and Levites, which is ascending to the Temple with the animals for sacrifice. With <reference osisRef="Ps.118.19">Psa 118:19</reference> the procession stands at the entrance. The second part (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.20-Ps.118.27">Psa 118:20-27</reference>) is sung by the body of Levites who receive the festive procession. Then <reference osisRef="Ps.118.28">Psa 118:28</reference> is the answer of those who have arrived, and <reference osisRef="Ps.118.29">Psa 118:29</reference> the concluding song of all of them. This antiphonal arrangement is recognised even by the Talmud (<hi type="italic">B. Pesachim</hi> 119 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) and Midrash. The whole Psalm, too, has moreover a peculiar formation. It resembles the <hi type="italic">Mashal</hi> Psalms, for each verse has of itself its completed sense, its own scent and hue; one thought is joined to another as branch to branch and flower to flower.
entries.d3f40789ebd6780807439fb05555a37eef3c1623: <reference osisRef="Ps.118.1-Ps.118.18">Psa 118:1-18</reference> <div eID="gen10116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10117" type="x-p"/> The Hodu-cry is addressed first of all and every one; then the whole body of the laity of Israel and the priests, and at last (as it appears) the proselytes (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11">Psa 115:9-11</reference>) who fear the God of revelation, are urgently admonished to echo it back; for “yea, His mercy endureth for ever,” is the required hypophon. In <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>, Israel too then begins as one man to praise the ever-gracious goodness of God. יהּ, the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> of which might easily become inaudible after קראתי, has an emphatic <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.18">Psa 118:18</reference></hi>, and המּצר has the orthophonic stroke beside צר (the so-called מקּל), which points to the correct tone-syllable of the word that has <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>.<note placement="foot">Vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 7 note, and p. 21, end of note 1.</note> <div eID="gen10117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10118" type="x-p"/> Instead of ענני it is here pointed ענני, which also occurs in other instances not only with distinctive, but also (though not uniformly) with conjunctive accents.<note placement="foot">Hitzig on <reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">Pro 8:22</reference> considers the pointing קנני to be occasioned by <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, and in fact ענני in the passage before us has <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>, and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference> <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>; but in the passage before us, if we read במרחביה as one word according to the Masora, ענני is rather to be accented with <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>; and in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference> the reading ענני is found side by side with ענני (e.g., in <hi type="italic">Bibl. Bomberg</hi>. 1521). Nevertheless צרפתני <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>, and הרני <reference osisRef="Job.30.19">Job 30:19</reference> (according to Kimchi’s <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi>, 30 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), beside <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>, show that the pointing beside conjunctive as beside disjunctive accents wavers between <hi type="italic">a&</hi> and <hi type="italic">a4</hi>, although <hi type="italic">a4</hi> is properly only justified beside disjunctive accents, and צוּני also really only occurs in pause.</note> <div eID="gen10118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10119" type="x-p"/> The constructions is a pregnant one (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.22">Psa 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.7">Psa 74:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.19">2Sa 18:19</reference>; Ezr 2:62; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.1">2Ch 32:1</reference>): He answered me by removing me to a free space (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.20">Psa 18:20</reference>). Both lines end with יהּ; nevertheless the reading במּרחביה is attested by the Masora (vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Psalterium</hi>, pp. 132f.), instead of בּמּרחב יהּ. It has its advocates even in the Talmud (<hi type="italic">B. Pesachim</hi> 117 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), and signifies a boundless extent, יה expressing the highest degree of comparison, like מאפּליה in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.31">Jer 2:31</reference>, the deepest darkness. Even the lxx appears to have read מרחביה thus as one word (εἰς πλατυσμόν, Symmachus εἰς εὐρυχωρίαν). The Targum and Jerome, however, render it as we do; it is highly improbable that in one and the same verse the divine name should not be intended to be used in the same force of meaning. <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1-Ps.56.13">Psa 56:1-13</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.10">Psa 56:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.5">Psa 56:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.12">Psa 56:12</reference>) echoes in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.6">Psa 118:6</reference>; and in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">Psa 118:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.54.6">Psa 54:6</reference>) is in the mind of the later poet. In that passage it is still more clear than in the passage before us that by the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּעזרי Jahve is not meant to be designated as <hi type="italic">unus e multis</hi>, but as a helper who outweighs the greatest multitude of helpers. The Jewish people had experienced this helpful succour of Jahve in opposition to the persecutions of the Samaritans and the satraps during the building of the Temple; and had at the same time learned what is expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7-Ps.118.8">Psa 118:7-8</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3">Psa 146:3</reference>), that trust in Jahve (for which חסה ב is the proper word) proves true, and trust in men, on the contrary, and especially in princes, is deceptive; for under Pseudo-Smerdis the work, begun under Cyrus, and represented as open to suspicion even in the reign of Cambyses, was interdicted. But in the reign of Darius it again became free: Jahve showed that He disposes events and the hearts of men in favour of His people, so that out of this has grown up in the minds of His people the confident expectation of a world-subduing supremacy expressed in Psa 118:10. <div eID="gen10119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10120" type="x-p"/> The clauses <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.10">Psa 118:10</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.11">Psa 118:11</reference></hi>, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference></hi>, expressed in the perfect form, are intended more hypothetically than as describing facts. The perfect is here set out in relief as a hypothetical tense by the following future. כּל־גּוים signifies, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.117.1">Psa 117:1</reference>, the heathen of every kind. דּברים (in the Aramaic and Arabic with )ז are both bees and wasps, which make themselves especially troublesome in harvest time. The suffix of אמילם (from מוּל = מלל, to hew down, cut in pieces) is the same as in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.30">Exo 29:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.2.17">Exo 2:17</reference>, and also beside a conjunctive accent in Psa 74:8. Yet the reading אמילם, like יחיתן <reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">Hab 2:17</reference>, is here the better supported (vid., Gesenius, <hi type="italic">Lehrgebäude</hi>, S. 177), and it has been adopted by Norzi, Heidenheim, and Baer. The כּי is that which states the ground or reason, and then becomes directly confirmatory and assuring (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">Psa 128:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.4">Psa 128:4</reference>), which here, after the “in the name of Jahve” that precedes it, is applied and placed just as in the oath in 1Sa 14:44. And in general, as Redslob has demonstrated, כּי has not originally a relative, but a positive (determining) signification, כ being just as much a demonstrative sound as ד, ז, שׁ, and ת (cf. ἐκεῖ, ἐκεῖνος, κει'νος, <hi type="italic">ecce, hic, illic</hi>, with the Doric τηνεί, τῆνος). The notion of compassing round about is heightened in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.11">Psa 118:11</reference> </hi>by the juxtaposition of two forms of the same verb (Ges. §67, rem. 10), as in Hos 4:18; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Hab 1:5</reference>; Zep 2:1, and frequently. The figure of the bees is taken from Deu 1:44. The perfect דּעכוּ (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.43.17">Isa 43:17</reference>) describes their destruction, which takes place instantly and unexpectedly. The <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> points to the punishing power that comes upon them: they are extinguished (<hi type="italic">exstinguuntur</hi>) like a fire of thorns, the crackling flame of which expires as quickly as it has blazed up (<reference osisRef="Ps.58.10">Psa 58:10</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.118.13">Psa 118:13</reference> the language of Israel is addressed to the hostile worldly power, as the antithesis shows. It thrust, yea thrust (<hi type="italic">inf. intens.</hi>) Israel, that it might fall (לנפּל; with reference to the pointing, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference>); but Jahve’s help would not suffer it to come to that pass. Therefore the song at the Red Sea is revived in the heart and mouth of Israel. <reference osisRef="Ps.118.14">Psa 118:14</reference> (like <reference osisRef="Isa.12.2">Isa 12:2</reference>) is taken from Exo 15:2. עזּי (in MSS also written עזּי) is a collateral form of עזּי (Ew. §255, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), and here signifies the lofty self-consciousness which is united with the possession of power: pride and its expression an exclamation of joy. Concerning זמרת vid., on Psa 16:6. As at that time, the cry of exultation and of salvation (i.e., of deliverance and of victory) is in the tabernacles of the righteous: the right hand of Jahve - they sing - עשׂה חיל (Num 24:18), practises valour, proves itself energetic, gains (maintains) the victory. רוממה is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, and therefore an adjective: <hi type="italic">victoriosa</hi> (Ew. §120 <hi type="italic">d</hi>), from רמם = רוּם like שׁומם from שׁמם. It is not the <hi type="italic">part. Pil.</hi> (cf. Hos 11:7), since the rejection of the participial <hi type="italic">Mem</hi> occurs in connection with <hi type="italic">Poal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pual</hi>, but not elsewhere with <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> (רומם = מרומם from רוּם). The word yields a simpler sense, too, as <hi type="italic">adject. participle Kal; romēmā́h</hi> is only the fuller form for <hi type="italic">ramā́h</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.8">Exo 14:8</reference> (cf. <hi type="italic">rā́mah</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa 26:11</reference>). It is not its own strength that avails for Israel’s exultation of victory, but the energy of the right hand of Jahve. Being come to the brink of the abyss, Israel is become anew sure of its immortality through Him. God has, it is true, most severely chastened it (יסּרנּי with the suffix <hi type="italic">anni</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Gen.30.6">Gen 30:6</reference>, and יהּ with the emphatic <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, which neither reduplicates nor connects, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Psa 94:12</reference>), but still with moderation (Isa 27:7.). He has not suffered Israel to fall a prey to death, but reserved it for its high vocation, that it may see the mighty deeds of God and proclaim them to all the world. Amidst such celebration of Jahve the festive procession of the dedication of the Temple has arrived at the enclosure wall of the Temple.
entries.f073cb2285a5c747e4a0254731ba7b05f872f39d: <reference osisRef="Ps.118.19-Ps.118.29">Psa 118:19-29</reference> <div eID="gen10120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10121" type="x-p"/> The gates of the Temple are called gates of righteousness because they are the entrance to the place of the mutual intercourse between God and His church in accordance with the order of salvation. First the “gates” are spoken of, and then the one “gate,” the principal entrance. Those entering in must be “righteous ones;” only conformity with a divine loving will gives the right to enter. With reference to the formation of the conclusion <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.118.19">Psa 118:19</reference></hi>, vid., Ew. §347, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. In the Temple-building Israel has before it a reflection of that which, being freed from the punishment it had had to endure, it is become through the mercy of its God. With the exultation of the multitude over the happy beginning of the rebuilding there was mingled, at the laying of the foundation-stone, the loud weeping of many of the grey-headed priests. Levites, and heads of the tribes who had also seen the first Temple (Ezr 3:12.). It was the troublous character of the present which made them thus sad in spirit; the consideration of the depressing circumstances of the time, the incongruity of which weighed so heavily upon their soul in connection with the remembrance of the former Temple, that memorably glorious monument of the royal power of David and Solomon.<note placement="foot">Kurtz, in combating our interpretation, reduces the number of the weeping ones to “some few,” but the narrative says the very opposite.</note> <div eID="gen10121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10122" type="x-p"/> And even further on there towered aloft before Zerubbabel, the leader of the building, a great mountain; gigantic difficulties and hindrances arose between the powerlessness of the present position of Zerubbabel and the completion of the building of the Temple, which had it is true been begun, but was impeded. This mountain God has made into a plain, and qualified Zerubbabel to bring forth the top and key-stone (האבן הראשׁה) out of its past concealment, and thus to complete the building, which is now consecrated amidst a loud outburst of incessant shouts of joy (Zec 4:7). <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference> points back to that disheartened disdain of the small troubles beginning which was at work among the builders (Ezr 3:10) at the laying of the foundation-stone, and then further at the interruption of the buidling. That rejected (disdained) corner-stone is nevertheless become ראשׁ פּנּהּ, i.e., the head-stone of the corner (<reference osisRef="Job.38.6">Job 38:6</reference>), which being laid upon the corner, supports and protects the stately edifice - an emblem of the power and dignity to which. <div eID="gen10122" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Israel has attained in the midst of the peoples out of deep humiliation.</title> <div sID="gen10123" type="x-p"/> In connection with this only indirect reference of the assertion to Israel we avoid the question - perplexing in connection with the direct reference to the people despised by the heathen - how can the heathen be called “the builders?” Kurtz answers: “For the building which the heathen world considers it to be its life’s mission and its mission in history to rear, viz., the Babel-tower of worldly power and worldly glory, they have neither been able nor willing to make use of Israel....” But this conjunction of ideas is devoid of scriptural support and without historical reality; for the empire of the world has set just as much value, according to political relations, upon the incorporation of Israel as upon that of every other people. Further, if what is meant is Israel’s own despising of the small beginning of a new ear that is dawning, it is then better explained as in connection with the reference of the declaration to Jesus the Christ in <reference osisRef="Matt.21.42-Matt.21.44">Mat 21:42-44</reference>; Mar 12:10., <reference osisRef="Acts.4.11">Act 4:11</reference> (ὑφ ̓ ὑμῶν τῶν οἰκοδομούντων), 1Pe 2:7, the builders are the chiefs and members of Israel itself, and not the heathen. From 1Pe 2:6; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.33">Rom 9:33</reference>, we see how this reference to Christ is brought about, viz., by means of <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>, where Jahve says: <hi type="italic">Behold I am He who hath laid in Zion a stone, a stone of trial, a precious corner-stone of well-founded founding - whoever believeth shall not totter.</hi> In the light of this Messianic prophecy of Isaiah <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference> of our Psalm also comes to have a Messianic meaning, which is warranted by the fact, that the history of Israel is recapitulated and culminates in the history of Christ; or, according to Joh 2:19-21 (cf. Zec 6:12.), still more accurately by the fact, that He who in His state of humiliation is the despised and rejected One is become in His state of glorification the eternal glorious Temple in which dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, and is united with humanity which has been once for all atoned for. In the joy of the church at the Temple of the body of Christ which arose after the three days of burial, the joy which is here typically expressed in the words: “From with Jahve, i.e., by the might which dwells with Him, is this come to pass, wonderful is it become (has it been carried out) in our eyes,” therefore received its fulfilment. It is not נפלאת but נפלאת, like הבאת in <reference osisRef="Gen.33.11">Gen 33:11</reference>, קראת from קרא = קרה in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.29">Deu 31:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.23">Jer 44:23</reference>, קראת from קרא, to call, Isa 7:14. We can hear <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">Isa 25:9</reference> sounding through this passage, as above in Psa 118:19., Isa 26:1. The God of Israel has given this turn, so full of glory for His people, to the history.<note placement="foot">The verse, “This is the day which the Lord hath made,” etc., was, according to Chrysostom, an ancient hypophon of the church. It has a glorious history.</note> <div eID="gen10123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10124" type="x-p"/> He is able now to plead for more distant salvation and prosperity with all the more fervent confidence. אנּא (six times אנּה) is, as in every other instance (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.116.4">Psa 116:4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>. הושׁיעה is accented regularly on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., and draws the following נא towards itself by means of <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conj.</hi>; הצליחה on the other hand is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> according to the Masora and other ancient testimonies, and נא is not dageshed, without Norzi being able to state any reason for this different accentuation. After this watchword of prayer of the thanksgiving feast, in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">Psa 118:26</reference> those who receive them bless those who are coming (הבּא with <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>) in the name of Jahve, i.e., bid them welcome in His name. <div eID="gen10124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10125" type="x-p"/> The expression “from the house of Jahve,” like “from the fountain of Israel” in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Psa 68:27</reference>, is equivalent to, ye who belong to His house and to the church congregated around it. In the mouth of the people welcoming Jesus as the Messiah, Hoosanna' was a “God save the king” (vid., on Ps 20:10); they scattered palm branches at the same time, like the <hi type="italic">lulabs</hi> at the joyous cry of the Feast of Tabernacles, and saluted Him with the cry, “Blessed is He who cometh in the name of the Lord,” as being the longed-for guest of the Feast (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.9">Mat 21:9</reference>). According to the Midrash, in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">Psa 118:26</reference> it is the people of Jerusalem who thus greet the pilgrims. In the original sense of the Psalm, however, it is the body of Levites and priests above on the Temple-hill who thus receive the congregation that has come up. The many animals for sacrifice which they brought with them are enumerated in Ezr 6:17. On the ground of the fact that Jahve has proved Himself to be אל, the absolutely mighty One, by having granted light to His people, viz., loving-kindness, liberty, and joy, there then issues forth the ejaculation, “Bind the sacrifice,” etc. The lxx renders συστήσασθε ἑορτὴν ἐν τοῖς πυκάζουσιν, which is reproduced by the <hi type="italic">Psalterium Romanum: constituite diem solemnem in confrequentationibus</hi>, as Eusebius, Theodoret, and Chrysostom (although the last waveringly) also interpret it; on the other hand, it is rendered by the <hi type="italic">psalterium Gallicum: in condensis</hi>, as Apollinaris and Jerome (<hi type="italic">in frondosis</hi>) also understand it. But much as Luther’s version, which follows the latter interpretation, “Adorn the feast with green branches even to the horns of the altar,” accords with our German taste, it is still untenable; for אסר cannot signify to encircle with garlands and the like, nor would it be altogether suited to חג in this signification.<note placement="foot">Symmachus has felt this, for instead of συστήσασθε ἑορτὴν ἐν τοῖς πυκάζουσιν (<hi type="italic">in condensis</hi>) of the lxx, he renders it, transposing the notions, συνδήσατε ἐν πανηγύρει πυκάσματα. Chrysostom interprets this: στεφανώματα καὶ κλάδους ἀνάψατε τῷ ναῷ, for Montfaucon, who regards this as the version of the <hi type="italic">Sexta</hi>, is in error.</note> <div eID="gen10125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10126" type="x-p"/> Thus then in this instance A. Lobwasser renders it comparatively more correctly, although devoid of taste: “The Lord is great and mighty of strength who lighteneth us all; <hi type="italic">fasten your bullocks to the horns beside the altar</hi>.” To the horns?! So even Hitzig and others render it. But such a “binding to” is unheard of. And can אסר עד possibly signify to bind on to anything? And what would be the object of binding them to the horns of the altar? In order that they might not run away?! Hengstenberg and von Lengerke at least disconnect the words “unto the horns of the altar” from any relation to this precautionary measure, by interpreting: until it (the animal for the festal sacrifice) is raised upon the horns of the altar and sacrificed. But how much is then imputed to these words! No indeed, חג denotes the animals for the feast-offering, and there was so vast a number of these (according to Ezra <hi type="italic">loc. cit.</hi> seven hundred and twelve) that the whole space of the court of the priests was full of them, and the binding of them consequently had to go on as far as to the horns of the altar. Ainsworth (1627) correctly renders: “unto the hornes, that is, all the Court over, untill you come even to the hornes of the altar, intending hereby many sacrifices or boughs.” The meaning of the call is therefore: Bring your hecatombs and make them ready for sacrifice.<note placement="foot">In the language of the Jewish ritual <hi type="italic">Isru-chag</hi> is become the name of the after-feast day which follows the last day of the feast. Ps 118 is the customary Psalm for the <hi type="italic">Isru-chag</hi> of all מועדים.</note> <div eID="gen10126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10127" type="x-p"/> The words “unto (as far as) the horns of the altar” have the principal accent. In v. 28 (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.15.2">Exo 15:2</reference>) the festal procession replies in accordance with the character of the feast, and then the Psalm closes, in correspondence with its beginning, with a <hi type="italic">Hodu</hi> in which all voices join.  <chapter eID="Ps.118"/> <div eID="gen10127" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 118
At the time when this psalm was penned, whenever that was, David having attained to the possession of royal power, and aware that he reigned for the common safety of the Church, calls upon all the children of Abraham to ponder attentively this grace. He also recounts his dangers, the magnitude and variety of which would have slain him a hundred times, had not God wonderfully succored him. From this it is obvious that he came to the throne of the kingdom, neither by his own policy, nor by the favor of men, nor by any human means. At the same time, he informs us that he did not rashly or by wicked intrigues rush forward and take forcible possession of the kingdom of Saul, but that he was appointed and established king by God himself. Let us remember that it was the design of the Spirit, under the figure of this temporal kingdom, to describe the eternal and spiritual kingdom of God’s Son, even as David represented his person.
Calvin ascribes this psalm to David; but, as it is without any title, it is uncertain who was its author. On this point, and the occasion of its composition, various opinions prevail among commentators. According to Hengstenberg, it celebrates the return of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, and the laying the foundation of the second temple; in support of which he refers to Ezra 3:11. Phillips thinks it “probable that it was written for the occasion when David was to be anointed at Hebron king over the tribes of Israel, (2 Samuel 5;) for, previously to his inauguration, he was subjected to many dangers, both from avowed foes, as well as from Saul and his party. He was exposed to the hostility of the Philistines (1 Samuel 29,) and the Amalekites, (1 Samuel 30;) from the former he escaped in safety, and the latter he overcame in battle. Again, although he had been long chosen king of Israel by God, for a considerable period he was exposed to a severe persecution; he was obliged to flee for safety from his country, and it was not till after the death of Saul that his troubles ceased, and he ascended the throne, which had long been his by Divine appointment. To David, therefore, at Hebron, this psalm will apply; for he could then say, ‘All nations compassed me about. The Lord hath chastised me, but he hath not given me over unto death. The stone which the builders refused is become the head-stone of the corner. This is the Lord’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.’” Some assign it to the time of Hezekiah; and others to that period of Israel’s history, which is adorned by the illustrious achievements of the Maccabees. “I shall not presume,” says Walford, “to decide which of these opinions is the most agreeable to truth. It will be more to our purpose to observe, that the psalm was read on occasion of a solemn procession that was formed by the king or chief magistrate, whoever he might be, the priests and the people at large, of all ranks, in order to perform public sacrifices of thanksgiving at the temple.”
Psalm 118:1-4
1. Praise ye Jehovah; because he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever. 2. Let Israel now
Horsley very properly translates the Hebrew word נא, na, in this and the two following verses, by O, instead of now: — “O, Let Israel say — O, Let the house of Aaron say — O, Let them that fear Jehovah say.” “The word now,” he observes, “in our language is a particle of entreaty, and is therefore used by our translators to express the supplicatory particle of the Hebrew language, נא. But though now, in our language, is indeed a particle of entreaty, it is only when the verb is in the imperative mood, and in the second person; as, ‘Do, now, grant me this favor;’ or, at least, in speaking to the person of whom the thing is asked. When נא is joined to a verb in the third person, or when the person who is to grant the petition, or perform the thing advised, is not immediately addressed, it should be rendered by some other word or phrase. ‘By all means,’ or ‘of all things,’ are equivalent phrases, in respect of the sense, but not sufficiently dignified to suit the style of sacred poetry. O is perhaps the best particle, in these cases, that our language furnishes.”
say, that his mercy endureth for ever. 3. Let the house of Aaron now say, that his mercy endureth for ever. 4. Let those who fear Jehovah now say, that his mercy endureth for ever.
 
1 Praise ye Jehovah In this passage we see that David does not merely in a private capacity render thanks to God, but that he loudly summons the people to engage in the common exercises of piety. This he does, not simply from his having been divinely appointed to be the captain and teacher of others; but, God having invested him with royal power, had manifested his sympathy with his distressed Church. Hence he exhorts the Israelites to magnify the grace of God, under whose kind protection he appears to re-establish them in safety. In the beginning of the psalm he alludes generally to the goodness and mercy of God, but he shortly instances himself as an evidence of his goodness, as will be seen in its proper place. It becomes us at present to recall to mind what I mentioned in the preceding psalm, that a reason for praising God is given to us on account of his mercy, in preference to his power or justice; because, though his glory shine forth in them also, yet will we never promptly and heartily sound forth his praises, until he win us by the sweetness of his goodness. Accordingly, in Psalm 51:17, we found that the lips of the faithful were opened to praise God, when they perceived that he was truly their deliverer. In restricting his address to Israel, and to the children of Aaron, he is guided by a regard to his own times, because, up to that period, the adoption did not extend beyond that one nation. He again resumes the order which he observed in Psalm 116:1; for, after exhorting the children of Abraham, who had been separated from the Gentiles by the election of God, and also the sons of Aaron, who, by virtue of the priesthood, ought to take the precedence in conducting the psalmody, he directs his discourse to the other worshippers of God; because there were many hypocrites among the Israelites, who, occupying a place in the Church, were yet strangers to it. This is not inconsistent with David’s here speaking by the spirit of prophecy, respecting the future kingdom of Christ. That kingdom, no doubt, extended to the Gentiles, but its commencement and first-fruits were among God’s chosen people.
Psalm 118:5-9
5. I called upon God in my distress, and God heard me, by setting me at large. 6. Jehovah is with me: ­I will not fear what man may do unto me. 7. Jehovah is with me among those who help me, and I shall see my desire upon mine enemies. 8. It is better to hope in Jehovah than to confide in man: 9. It is better to hope in Jehovah than to confide in princes.
